claim: The NAD+ precursor NMN activates dSarm to trigger axon degeneration in Drosophila.
source: The NAD+ precursor NMN activates dSarm to trigger axon degeneration in Drosophila
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the title and supported throughout the manuscript with experimental data.

claim: Lowering NMN levels in Drosophila through the expression of prokaryotic NMN-Deamidase (NMN-D) preserves severed axons for months.
source: Here, we demonstrate that lowering NMN levels in Drosophila through the expression of a newly generated prokaryotic NMN-Deamidase (NMN-D) preserves severed axons for months and keeps them circuit-integrated for weeks.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing axon preservation at 10, 30, and 50 days post axotomy in Figure 1E.

claim: NMN-D keeps severed axons circuit-integrated for weeks.
source: Here, we demonstrate that lowering NMN levels in Drosophila through the expression of a newly generated prokaryotic NMN-Deamidase (NMN-D) preserves severed axons for months and keeps them circuit-integrated for weeks.
evidence: Supported by optogenetic experiments showing preserved synaptic connectivity at 7 and 14 days post axotomy in Figure 3.

claim: NMN-D alters the NAD+ metabolic flux by lowering NMN, while NAD+ remains unchanged in vivo.
source: NMN-D alters the NAD+ metabolic flux by lowering NMN, while NAD+ remains unchanged in vivo.
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS metabolite measurements in fly heads showing sixfold lower NMN levels and unchanged NAD+ levels in Figure 2B.

claim: Increased NMN synthesis by the expression of mouse nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (mNAMPT) leads to faster axon degeneration after injury.
source: Increased NMN synthesis by the expression of mouse nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (mNAMPT) leads to faster axon degeneration after injury.
evidence: Supported by wing injury assay data showing signs of degeneration at 4 hours post axotomy with mNAMPT expression versus 6 hours for controls in Figure 4D and E.

claim: NMN-induced activation of dSarm mediates axon degeneration in vivo.
source: We also show that NMN-induced activation of dSarm mediates axon degeneration in vivo.
evidence: Supported by NADase activity assays showing NMN-dependent activation of wild-type dSarm but not K450R mutant in Figure 5C, and rescue experiments in Figure 5E.

claim: NMN-D delays neurodegeneration caused by loss of the sole NMN-consuming and NAD+-synthesizing enzyme dNmnat.
source: Finally, NMN-D delays neurodegeneration caused by loss of the sole NMN-consuming and NAD+-synthesizing enzyme dNmnat.
evidence: Supported by time course experiments showing dnmnat1 mutant neurons with NMN-D remain intact for 5 days before degenerating in Figure 6C.

claim: Axon degeneration contributes to the disruption of neuronal circuit function in diseased and injured nervous systems.
source: Axon degeneration contributes to the disruption of neuronal circuit function in diseased and injured nervous systems.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations to the literature.

claim: Severed axons degenerate following the activation of an evolutionarily conserved signaling pathway.
source: Severed axons degenerate following the activation of an evolutionarily conserved signaling pathway, which culminates in the activation of SARM1 in mammals to execute the pathological depletion of the metabolite NAD+.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by the context of the introduction.

claim: The evolutionarily conserved signaling pathway culminates in the activation of SARM1 in mammals to execute the pathological depletion of NAD+.
source: Severed axons degenerate following the activation of an evolutionarily conserved signaling pathway, which culminates in the activation of SARM1 in mammals to execute the pathological depletion of the metabolite NAD+.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: SARM1 NADase activity is activated by the NAD+ precursor nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN).
source: SARM1 NADase activity is activated by the NAD+ precursor nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations in the abstract.

claim: In mammals, keeping NMN levels low potently preserves axons after injury.
source: In mammals, keeping NMN levels low potently preserves axons after injury.
evidence: This is established knowledge from mammalian studies cited in the abstract.

claim: The elimination of large portions of axons is a widespread event in the developing nervous system.
source: The elimination of large portions of axons is a widespread event in the developing nervous system (Neukomm and Freeman, 2014; Riccomagno and Kolodkin, 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Axon degeneration is an early hallmark of nervous system injury.
source: Axon degeneration is also an early hallmark of nervous system injury and a common feature of neurodegenerative diseases (Coleman and Höke, 2020; Mariano et al., 2018; Merlini et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Axon degeneration is a common feature of neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Axon degeneration is also an early hallmark of nervous system injury and a common feature of neurodegenerative diseases (Coleman and Höke, 2020; Mariano et al., 2018; Merlini et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Wallerian degeneration is a well-established, evolutionarily conserved, and simple system to study how injured axons execute their self-destruction.
source: Wallerian degeneration is a well-established, evolutionarily conserved, and simple system to study how injured axons execute their self-destruction (Llobet Rosell and Neukomm, 2019; Waller, 1850).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Upon axonal injury (axotomy), distal axons separated from their soma degenerate within a day.
source: Upon axonal injury (axotomy), distal axons separated from their soma degenerate within a day.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Wallerian degeneration.

claim: Axotomy activates a signaling pathway (programmed axon degeneration, or axon death) that actively executes the self-destruction of severed axons.
source: Axotomy activates a signaling pathway (programmed axon degeneration, or axon death) that actively executes the self-destruction of severed axons.
evidence: This is established knowledge about axon death signaling.

claim: Induced signaling culminates in the activation of sterile alpha and TIR motif-containing protein 1 (dSarm and SARM1 in flies and mice, respectively).
source: Induced signaling culminates in the activation of sterile alpha and TIR motif-containing protein 1 (dSarm and SARM1 in flies and mice, respectively) (Gerdts et al., 2013; Osterloh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Once activated, dSarm/SARM1 executes the pathological depletion of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) in severed axons, culminating in catastrophic fragmentation.
source: As NADase, once activated, dSarm/SARM1 executes the pathological depletion of nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) in severed axons, culminating in catastrophic fragmentation (Essuman et al., 2017; Figley et al., 2021; Gerdts et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Axon death signaling is activated in many non-injury neurological disorders.
source: Initially thought to be activated only after injury, evidence accumulated over recent years that axon death signaling is also activated in many non-injury neurological disorders (Figley and DiAntonio, 2020; Hopkins et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: In mammals, SARM1 activation is tightly controlled by metabolites in the NAD+ biosynthetic pathway.
source: In mammals, SARM1 activation is tightly controlled by metabolites in the NAD+ biosynthetic pathway.
evidence: This is established knowledge from mammalian studies.

claim: The labile enzyme nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferase 2 (NMNAT2) is constantly transported into the axon, where it is degraded by the E3 ubiquitin ligase PAM-Highwire-Rpm-1 (PHR1) and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling.
source: The labile enzyme nicotinamide mononucleotide adenylyltransferase 2 (NMNAT2) is constantly transported into the axon, where it is degraded by the E3 ubiquitin ligase PAM-Highwire-Rpm-1 (PHR1) and mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling (Babetto et al., 2013; Gilley and Coleman, 2010; Walker et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Upon axonal injury, axonal transport halts and NMNAT2 is rapidly degraded, leading to a temporal rise of axonal NMN and a halt in NAD+ biosynthesis.
source: Upon axonal injury, axonal transport halts. Subsequently, NMNAT2 is rapidly degraded. It leads to a temporal rise of axonal NMN and a halt in NAD+ biosynthesis (Di Stefano et al., 2017; Di Stefano et al., 2015; Loreto et al., 2021; Loreto et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: NMN and NAD+ compete by binding to an allosteric pocket in the SARM1 armadillo-repeat (ARM) domain, which is crucial for SARM1 activation.
source: NMN and NAD+ compete by binding to an allosteric pocket in the SARM1 armadillo-repeat (ARM) domain, which is crucial for SARM1 activation.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: A rise in NMN activates SARM1 by inducing its conformational change.
source: While a rise in NMN activates SARM1 by inducing its conformational change (Bratkowski et al., 2020; Figley et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2019), NAD+ prevents this activation by competing for the same pocket in the ARM domain (Jiang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: NAD+ prevents SARM1 activation by competing for the same pocket in the ARM domain.
source: While a rise in NMN activates SARM1 by inducing its conformational change (Bratkowski et al., 2020; Figley et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2019), NAD+ prevents this activation by competing for the same pocket in the ARM domain (Jiang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: The competitive binding of NMN and NAD+ to SARM1 occurs at physiologically relevant levels.
source: This competitive binding occurs at physiologically relevant levels of NMN and NAD+ (Angeletti et al., 2022).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: Expression of the prokaryotic enzyme PncC (NMN-Deamidase) converts NMN to nicotinic acid mononucleotide (NaMN).
source: Previous studies have shown that expression of the prokaryotic enzyme PncC–also known as NMN-Deamidase (NMNd)–converts NMN to nicotinic acid mononucleotide (NaMN) (Galeazzi et al., 2011), prevents SARM1 activation and preserves severed axons in mammals and zebrafish
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: PncC/NMN-Deamidase prevents SARM1 activation and preserves severed axons in mammals and zebrafish.
source: Previous studies have shown that expression of the prokaryotic enzyme PncC–also known as NMN-Deamidase (NMNd)–converts NMN to nicotinic acid mononucleotide (NaMN) (Galeazzi et al., 2011), prevents SARM1 activation and preserves severed axons in mammals and zebrafish: for instance, axons with NMNd remain preserved up to 96 hr in murine neuronal cultures (Di Stefano et al., 2015; Loreto et al., 2015; Sasaki et al., 2016), 24 hr in zebrafish and 3 weeks in mice (Di Stefano et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Axons with NMNd remain preserved up to 96 hr in murine neuronal cultures.
source: for instance, axons with NMNd remain preserved up to 96 hr in murine neuronal cultures (Di Stefano et al., 2015; Loreto et al., 2015; Sasaki et al., 2016), 24 hr in zebrafish and 3 weeks in mice (Di Stefano et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Axons with NMNd remain preserved 24 hr in zebrafish.
source: for instance, axons with NMNd remain preserved up to 96 hr in murine neuronal cultures (Di Stefano et al., 2015; Loreto et al., 2015; Sasaki et al., 2016), 24 hr in zebrafish and 3 weeks in mice (Di Stefano et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: Axons with NMNd remain preserved 3 weeks in mice.
source: for instance, axons with NMNd remain preserved up to 96 hr in murine neuronal cultures (Di Stefano et al., 2015; Loreto et al., 2015; Sasaki et al., 2016), 24 hr in zebrafish and 3 weeks in mice (Di Stefano et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: Much of the axon death signaling mechanism is conserved in Drosophila.
source: Much of this mechanism of axon death signaling is conserved in Drosophila (Llobet Rosell and Neukomm, 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: Flies harbor a single dnmnat gene that provides a cytoplasmic and nuclear splice protein variant.
source: A single dnmnat gene provides a cytoplasmic and nuclear splice protein variant; consequently, dnmnat disruption results in cellular dNmnat loss (Ruan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: dnmnat disruption results in cellular dNmnat loss.
source: A single dnmnat gene provides a cytoplasmic and nuclear splice protein variant; consequently, dnmnat disruption results in cellular dNmnat loss (Ruan et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: dNmnat turnover is regulated solely by the E3 ubiquitin ligase Highwire (Hiw) but not by MAPK signaling.
source: dNmnat turnover is regulated solely by the E3 ubiquitin ligase Highwire (Hiw) (Xiong et al., 2012) but not by MAPK signaling (Neukomm et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: The BTB/Back domain-containing Axundead (Axed) executes catastrophic fragmentation downstream of NAD+ depletion.
source: Furthermore, the BTB/Back domain-containing Axundead (Axed) executes catastrophic fragmentation downstream of NAD+ depletion, while the mammalian paralog(s) remain to be identified (Neukomm et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: The mammalian paralog(s) of Axed remain to be identified.
source: Furthermore, the BTB/Back domain-containing Axundead (Axed) executes catastrophic fragmentation downstream of NAD+ depletion, while the mammalian paralog(s) remain to be identified (Neukomm et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: Flies lack nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT).
source: Flies lack nicotinamide phosphoribosyltransferase (NAMPT) (Gossmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: Gal4/UAS-mediated NMNd expression in Drosophila neurons preserves severed axons for 3–5 days after injury.
source: The Gal4/UAS-mediated NMNd expression in Drosophila neurons preserves severed axons for 3–5 days after injury (Hsu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in hiw, dsarm, and axed, as well as over-expression of dnmnat, result in severed axons that remain preserved for weeks to months.
source: It contrasts with the phenotype of other axon death signaling mediators, such as loss-of-function mutations in hiw, dsarm, and axed, as well as over-expression of dnmnat (dnmnatOE), all of which harbor severed axons that remain preserved for weeks to months (Fang et al., 2012; Neukomm et al., 2017; Neukomm et al., 2014; Osterloh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: Wild-type and enzymatically dead NMN-D enzymes are equally expressed in S2 cells.
source: We found that wild-type and enzymatically dead NMN-D enzymes are equally expressed in S2 cells, as detected by our newly generated anti-PncC/NMNd/NMN-D antibodies (Materials and methods, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: NMN-D and NMN-Ddead immunoreactivities were significantly stronger than NMNd in fly heads.
source: We found that NMN-D and NMN-Ddead immunoreactivities were significantly stronger than NMNd (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot and quantification data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: GFP immunoreactivity was detected in NMN-D and NMN-Ddead, confirming the robust expression of the newly generated tagged proteins.
source: In addition, GFP immunoreactivity was also detected in NMN-D and NMN-Ddead, confirming the robust expression of the newly generated tagged proteins (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data in Figure 1A.

claim: Severed axons with GFP or NMN-Ddead degenerated at 7 days post axotomy.
source: While severed axons with GFP or NMN-Ddead degenerated, axons with NMN-D remained fully preserved at 7 dpa (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by wing injury assay data in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Axons with NMN-D remained fully preserved at 7 days post axotomy.
source: While severed axons with GFP or NMN-Ddead degenerated, axons with NMN-D remained fully preserved at 7 dpa (Figure 1B and C, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by wing injury assay data in Figure 1B and C.

claim: Strong preservation was seen in cholinergic olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs), where severed axons with NMN-D remained preserved at 7 days post axotomy.
source: Similarly, strong preservation was seen in cholinergic olfactory receptor neurons (ORNs), where severed axons with NMN-D remained preserved at 7 dpa (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by antennal ablation assay data in Figure 1D.

claim: Severed preserved axons were observed in all 10, 30, and 50 days post axotomy brains.
source: We extended the ORN injury assay and found preservation at 10, 30, and 50 dpa (Figure 1E). While quantifying the precise number of axons is technically not feasible, severed preserved axons were observed in all 10, 30, and 50 dpa brains, albeit fewer at later time points (MacDonald et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by antennal ablation assay data in Figure 1E.

claim: NAD+ can be synthesized from nicotinamide (NAM), nicotinamide riboside (NR), and quinolinate in fly heads.
source: We confirmed that NAD+ can be synthesized from nicotinamide (NAM), nicotinamide riboside (NR), and quinolinate.
evidence: Supported by enzymatic activity assays in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The Drosophila Qaprt homolog that catalyzes the conversion from quinolinate to nicotinic acid mononucleotide (NaMN) remains to be identified.
source: However, the Drosophila Qaprt homolog that catalyzes the conversion from quinolinate to nicotinic acid mononucleotide (NaMN) remains to be identified (Katsyuba et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: The absence of NAMPT activity was confirmed in fly heads.
source: We also confirmed the absence of NAMPT activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Gossmann et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by enzymatic activity assays in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and cited reference.

claim: The expression of NMN-D results in sixfold lower NMN levels in fly heads.
source: Consistent with robust NMN-D activity, NMN levels were sixfold lower and NaMN 12-fold higher.
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS metabolite measurements in Figure 2B.

claim: The expression of NMN-D results in 12-fold higher NaMN levels in fly heads.
source: Consistent with robust NMN-D activity, NMN levels were sixfold lower and NaMN 12-fold higher.
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS metabolite measurements in Figure 2B.

claim: The expression of NMN-D results in significantly higher NaAD and NaR levels in fly heads.
source: We also found significantly higher NaAD and NaR levels.
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS metabolite measurements in Figure 2B.

claim: All other metabolites remained unchanged with NMN-D expression, including NAD+.
source: Importantly, all other metabolites remained unchanged, including NAD+ (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS metabolite measurements in Figure 2B.

claim: Besides the expected significant increase of the Gal4-mediated expression of NMN-D and NMN-Ddead, no notable changes in gene expression were observed.
source: However, besides the expected significant increase of the Gal4-mediated expression of NMN-D and NMN-Ddead, we did not observe any notable changes (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Flies expressing GFP in JO neurons failed to elicit antennal grooming following red-light exposure at 7 days post axotomy.
source: Flies expressing GFP in JO neurons failed to elicit antennal grooming following red-light exposure at 7 dpa (Figure 3, Video 1).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic assay data in Figure 3.

claim: Flies with JO-specific NMN-D expression continued to elicit antennal grooming at 7 days post axotomy.
source: In contrast, flies with JO-specific NMN-D expression continued to elicit antennal grooming at 7 dpa (Figure 3, Video 2).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic assay data in Figure 3.

claim: The evoked grooming behavior remained equally robust at 14 days post axotomy in flies with NMN-D expression.
source: Remarkably, the evoked grooming behavior remained equally robust at 14 dpa (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic assay data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Flies expressing NMN-Ddead in JO neurons failed to elicit antennal grooming upon red-light exposure at 7 days post axotomy.
source: Preservation of synaptic connectivity depended on low NMN levels, as flies expressing NMN-Ddead in JO neurons failed to elicit antennal grooming upon red-light exposure at 7 dpa (Figure 3, Video 3).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic assay data in Figure 3.

claim: NAM, NMN, and NAD+ levels remained unchanged under physiological conditions with mNAMPT expression.
source: Surprisingly, NAM, NMN, and NAD+ levels remained unchanged under physiological conditions (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS metabolite measurements in Figure 4C.

claim: mNAMPT overexpression resulted in threefold higher NR levels.
source: However, we noticed threefold higher NR and a moderate but significant elevation of ADPR and cADPR levels upon mNAMPT overexpression (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS metabolite measurements in Figure 4C.

claim: mNAMPT overexpression resulted in a moderate but significant elevation of ADPR and cADPR levels.
source: However, we noticed threefold higher NR and a moderate but significant elevation of ADPR and cADPR levels upon mNAMPT overexpression (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS/MS metabolite measurements in Figure 4C.

claim: Besides the expected significant increase in the Gal4-mediated expression of mNAMPT, no notable changes at the mRNA level were observed.
source: Besides the expected significant increase in the Gal4-mediated expression of mNAMPT, we did not observe any notable changes at the mRNA level (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Axons with GFP showed signs of degeneration starting from 6 hr post axotomy.
source: Strikingly, in our wing injury assay, while axons with GFP showed signs of degeneration starting from 6 hr post axotomy (hpa), mNAMPT expression resulted in significantly faster axon degeneration with signs of degeneration at 4 hpa (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: Supported by wing injury assay data in Figure 4D and E.

claim: mNAMPT expression resulted in significantly faster axon degeneration with signs of degeneration at 4 hr post axotomy.
source: Strikingly, in our wing injury assay, while axons with GFP showed signs of degeneration starting from 6 hr post axotomy (hpa), mNAMPT expression resulted in significantly faster axon degeneration with signs of degeneration at 4 hpa (Figure 4D and E).
evidence: Supported by wing injury assay data in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Mutations in dsarm and hiw completely blocked the degeneration of severed axons expressing mNAMPT.
source: While mutations in dsarm and hiw completely blocked the degeneration of severed axons expressing mNAMPT, axed showed a partial preservation of 60% at 12 hr after injury (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by wing injury assay data in Figure 4F.

claim: axed showed a partial preservation of 60% at 12 hr after injury in axons expressing mNAMPT.
source: While mutations in dsarm and hiw completely blocked the degeneration of severed axons expressing mNAMPT, axed showed a partial preservation of 60% at 12 hr after injury (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by wing injury assay data in Figure 4F.

claim: axed mutants, in the absence of mNAMPT expression, showed a similar preservation within the first 12 hr.
source: Importantly, axed mutants, in the absence of mNAMPT expression, showed a similar preservation within the first 12 hr (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by wing injury assay data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: mNAMPT expression does not change the preservation provided by axed, dsarm, and hiw at 7 days post axotomy.
source: This preservation remained unchanged at 7 dpa, suggesting that mNAMPT expression does not change the preservation provided by axed, dsarm, and hiw (Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by wing injury assay data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2 and Figure 4G.

claim: A cell-permeable form of NMN (CZ-48) binds to and activates SARM1 by changing its conformation.
source: A cell-permeable form of NMN (CZ-48) binds to and activates SARM1 by changing its conformation (Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: Crystal structures of the ARM domain of dSarm (dSarmARM), as well as the full-length human SARM1 (hSARM1), support the observation that NMN acts as a ligand for dSarmARM.
source: Crystal structures of the ARM domain of dSarm (dSarmARM), as well as the full-length human SARM1 (hSARM1), support the observation that NMN acts as a ligand for dSarmARM (Figley et al., 2021; Gu et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: NMN binding to the ARM domain requires a critical residue, lysine 193 (K193), to induce a conformational change in the ARM domain of dSarm/SARM1.
source: NMN binding to the ARM domain requires a critical residue, lysine 193 (K193), to induce a conformational change in the ARM domain of dSarm/SARM1.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations in the results section.

claim: A mutation of the lysine residue (e.g. K193R) results in a dominant-negative injury-induced axon degeneration phenotype in murine cell cultures.
source: Consistent with this, a mutation of the lysine residue (e.g. K193R) results in a dominant-negative injury-induced axon degeneration phenotype in murine cell cultures (Bratkowski et al., 2020; Figley et al., 2021; Geisler et al., 2019; Loreto et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: An isoform dSarm(D) fails to fully rescue the dsarm896 defective axon death phenotype.
source: Crucially, an isoform we used previously, dSarm(D), fails to fully rescue the dsarm896 defective axon death phenotype (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B, Neukomm et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Wild-type and K450R dSarm(E) had similar constitutive NADase activities in the presence of 25 µM NAD+ alone.
source: While wild-type and K450R dSarm(E) had similar constitutive activities in the presence of 25 µM NAD+ alone, we found that only wild-type NADase activity was induced further with the addition of 50 µM NMN. At the same time, K450R remained essentially unchanged (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by NADase activity assay data in Figure 5C.

claim: Only wild-type dSarm(E) NADase activity was induced further with the addition of 50 µM NMN, while K450R remained essentially unchanged.
source: While wild-type and K450R dSarm(E) had similar constitutive activities in the presence of 25 µM NAD+ alone, we found that only wild-type NADase activity was induced further with the addition of 50 µM NMN. At the same time, K450R remained essentially unchanged (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by NADase activity assay data in Figure 5C.

claim: The expression of wild-type dSarm(E) (both tagged and untagged) almost entirely rescued dsarm896 mutants.
source: We found that the expression of wild-type dSarm(E) (both tagged and untagged) almost entirely rescued dsarm896 mutants, whereas dSarm(EK450R) proteins completely failed to rescue the phenotype at 7 dpe (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data in Figure 5E.

claim: dSarm(EK450R) proteins completely failed to rescue the dsarm896 phenotype at 7 days post eclosion.
source: We found that the expression of wild-type dSarm(E) (both tagged and untagged) almost entirely rescued dsarm896 mutants, whereas dSarm(EK450R) proteins completely failed to rescue the phenotype at 7 dpe (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by rescue experiment data in Figure 5E.

claim: The 100% preservation provided by NMN-D was partially reduced to 60% by nadsynRNAi at 7 days post axotomy.
source: At 7 dpa, the 100% preservation provided by NMN-D was partially reduced to 60% by nadsynRNAi in vivo (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by wing injury assay data in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: dsarm∆ARM clones with forced NAD+ depletion rapidly degenerated within 5 days after adults were born.
source: dsarm∆ARM clones with forced NAD+ depletion rapidly degenerated within 5 days after adults were born (days post eclosion, dpe) (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by time course data in Figure 6A.

claim: Lowering NMN levels by NMN-D in dsarm∆ARM clones did not alter the kinetics of neurodegeneration.
source: As expected, lowering NMN levels by NMN-D in dsarm∆ARM clones did not alter the kinetics of neurodegeneration (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by time course data in Figure 6A.

claim: The attenuated axon death phenotype of low NMN did not change in axed, dsarm, double mutants, hiw, and dnmnatOE backgrounds at 7 days post eclosion.
source: As expected, the attenuated axon death phenotype of low NMN did not change in these mutant backgrounds at 7 dpe (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by epistasis analysis data in Figure 6B.

claim: dnmnat1 mutant clones lack NMN consumption and NAD+ synthesis.
source: dNmnat is the sole enzyme with NAD+ biosynthetic activity in Drosophila. dnmnat1 mutant clones lack NMN consumption and NAD+ synthesis (Zhai et al., 2006), and they degenerate with similar kinetics as dsarm∆ARM clones (Neukomm et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: dnmnat1 mutant clones degenerate with similar kinetics as dsarm∆ARM clones.
source: dNmnat is the sole enzyme with NAD+ biosynthetic activity in Drosophila. dnmnat1 mutant clones lack NMN consumption and NAD+ synthesis (Zhai et al., 2006), and they degenerate with similar kinetics as dsarm∆ARM clones (Neukomm et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: Between 1–5 days post eclosion, while clones with dnmnat1 fully degenerated, NMN-D expressing dnmnat1 clones remained morphologically intact, similar to controls.
source: Between 1–5 dpe, while clones with dnmnat1 fully degenerated, NMN-D expressing dnmnat1 clones remained morphologically intact, similar to controls. After 5 days, these clones gradually started to deteriorate (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by time course data in Figure 6C.

claim: After 5 days, NMN-D expressing dnmnat1 clones gradually started to deteriorate.
source: Between 1–5 dpe, while clones with dnmnat1 fully degenerated, NMN-D expressing dnmnat1 clones remained morphologically intact, similar to controls. After 5 days, these clones gradually started to deteriorate (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by time course data in Figure 6C.

claim: The expression of NMN-Ddead completely failed to protect dnmnat1 neurons.
source: This protective delay of neurodegeneration depends on lowering NMN levels, as the expression of NMN-Ddead completely failed to protect dnmnat1 neurons (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by time course data in Figure 6C.

claim: Neurons with CRISPR/Cas9-targeted dnmnat degenerated as fast as dnmnat1 mutants.
source: Neurons with CRISPR/Cas9-targeted dnmnat degenerated as fast as dnmnat1 mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by time course data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Reduced synaptic connectivity was observed in 7- and 14-day-old flies with CRISPR/Cas9-targeted dnmnat.
source: In line with these findings, we observed reduced synaptic connectivity in 7- and 14-day-old flies (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic assay data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The expression of NMN-D in dnmnatsgRNAs clones resulted in similar neuroprotection as observed with dnmnat1 mutants.
source: We also found the expression of NMN-D in dnmnatsgRNAs clones resulted in similar neuroprotection as observed with dnmnat1 mutants. They remained morphologically intact during the first 5 days and then gradually degenerated (Figure 6—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by time course data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1F.

claim: NMN is a key mediator of axon degeneration in Drosophila, acting as an activator of dSarm in the axon death pathway in vivo.
source: Our data indicate that NMN is a key mediator of axon degeneration in Drosophila, acting as an activator of dSarm in the axon death pathway in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Lowering NMN levels has an equally potent protective effect as loss-of-function mutations in hiw, dsarm, and axed, as well as dnmnat over-expression.
source: We now show that lowering NMN levels has an equally potent protective effect, adding NMN as an additional mediator to the signaling pathway.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from comparing the preservation phenotypes across different genetic manipulations.

claim: Synaptic connectivity of severed axons is preserved for weeks with low NMN, comparable to hiw, dsarm, and axed mutants.
source: Synaptic connectivity of severed axons is also preserved for weeks, comparable to hiw, dsarm, and axed mutants (Neukomm et al., 2017), and dnmnat over-expression (Paglione et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic assay data and comparison with cited references.

claim: NMN is present in flies.
source: However, we provide compelling evidence that NMN is not only present in flies as previously reported (Lehmann et al., 2017) but that its accumulation causes axon degeneration.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: NMN accumulation causes axon degeneration in flies.
source: However, we provide compelling evidence that NMN is not only present in flies as previously reported (Lehmann et al., 2017) but that its accumulation causes axon degeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The difference in preservation between NMNd and NMN-D is likely due to the N-terminal GFP tag in GFP::NMN-D, which can increase protein stability.
source: This difference is likely due to the N-terminal GFP tag in GFP::NMN-D, which can increase protein stability (Rücker et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed expression differences and cited reference.

claim: NMN-D expression levels dictate the reduction of NMN, and therefore the preservation of severed axons.
source: This is supported by our newly generated anti-PncC antibodies and suggests that NMN-D expression levels dictate the reduction of NMN, and therefore the preservation of severed axons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between expression levels and preservation phenotypes.

claim: Mammals synthesize NMN with two distinct enzymatic reactions: NR consumption by NRK1/2 and NAM consumption by NAMPT.
source: Mammals synthesize NMN with two distinct enzymatic reactions: NR consumption by NRK1/2 and NAM consumption by NAMPT, both ensuring NMN supply.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian NAD+ metabolism.

claim: In Drosophila, NAMPT activity is absent, and NMN appears to be synthesized by Nrk alone.
source: In Drosophila, NAMPT activity is absent, and NMN appears to be synthesized by Nrk alone, yet dietary NMN supplementation might also contribute to NMN levels (Yoshino et al., 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference and data in the manuscript.

claim: NMNAT2 is rapidly disappearing in severed axons.
source: However, NMNAT2 is rapidly disappearing in severed axons (Gilley and Coleman, 2010), and so is dNmnat in Drosophila axons and synapses (Xiong et al., 2012), through PHR1 and Hiw, respectively, while NAMPT persists longer (Di Stefano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited references.

claim: dNmnat is rapidly disappearing in Drosophila axons and synapses through PHR1 and Hiw, respectively.
source: However, NMNAT2 is rapidly disappearing in severed axons (Gilley and Coleman, 2010), and so is dNmnat in Drosophila axons and synapses (Xiong et al., 2012), through PHR1 and Hiw, respectively, while NAMPT persists longer (Di Stefano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: NAMPT persists longer than NMNAT2 in severed axons.
source: However, NMNAT2 is rapidly disappearing in severed axons (Gilley and Coleman, 2010), and so is dNmnat in Drosophila axons and synapses (Xiong et al., 2012), through PHR1 and Hiw, respectively, while NAMPT persists longer (Di Stefano et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited reference.

claim: Persisting mNAMPT in severed Drosophila axons continues NMN synthesis, leading to faster NMN accumulation, dSarm activation, and faster axon degeneration.
source: It is therefore likely that persisting mNAMPT in severed Drosophila axons continues NMN synthesis, leading to faster NMN accumulation, dSarm activation, and faster axon degeneration.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed faster degeneration with mNAMPT expression and established knowledge about protein stability.

claim: The simultaneous manipulation of NMN and NAD+ levels supports that the competition between NMN and NAD+ is crucial in Drosophila to regulate dSarm activity and axon degeneration after axotomy in vivo.
source: Our simultaneous manipulation of NMN and NAD+ levels (by NMN-D expression and nadsynRNAi, respectively) further supports that this competition is crucial in Drosophila to regulate dSarm activity and, consequentially, axon degeneration after axotomy in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing partial reversion of NMN-D protection by nadsynRNAi.

claim: dNmnat is essential for NAD+ synthesis.
source: dNmnat is essential for NAD+ synthesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about dNmnat function.

claim: A rise in NMN, rather than the lack of NAD+ biosynthesis, is a trigger for neurons to degenerate in the dnmnat1 model, at least within the first 5 days.
source: Our results suggest that a rise in NMN, rather than the lack of NAD+ biosynthesis, is a trigger for neurons to degenerate also in this model, at least within the first 5 days.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that NMN-D delays dnmnat1-induced neurodegeneration.

claim: Once NAD+ levels drop beyond neuronal survival, neurons eventually degenerate.
source: Once NAD+ levels drop beyond neuronal survival, neurons eventually degenerate.
evidence: This is an inference based on the eventual degeneration of NMN-D expressing dnmnat1 neurons after 5 days.

claim: Neurons lacking NAD+ synthesis can survive for days.
source: Still, it is surprising to observe that neurons lacking NAD+ synthesis can survive for days.
evidence: This is an observation from the dnmnat1 + NMN-D experiments.

claim: The NAD+ turnover is slower than expected or mechanisms are in place to compensate for NAD+ loss, at least in the short term.
source: It suggests either that the NAD+ turnover is slower than expected (Liu et al., 2018) or mechanisms are in place to compensate for NAD+ loss, at least in the short term.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation that neurons can survive for days without NAD+ synthesis.

claim: NMN is a potent mediator of axon- and neurodegeneration in Drosophila.
source: In conclusion, NMN is a potent mediator of axon- and neurodegeneration in Drosophila.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Drosophila serves as an excellent model system to study NAD+ metabolism in vivo.
source: Our metabolic analyses further demonstrate that Drosophila serves as an excellent model system to study NAD+ metabolism in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the successful metabolic analyses performed in fly heads.
